title: TALCO: Tiling Genome Sequence Alignment Using Convergence of Traceback Pointers
problem: Long sequence alignments require excessive memory for hardware accelerators. Existing tiling heuristics reduce memory but degrade alignment quality, creating a critical tradeoff that limits hardware accelerator adoption in bioinformatics.
motivation: Third-generation sequencing technologies and growing whole-genome datasets make sequence alignment increasingly computationally demanding and require efficient hardware acceleration without sacrificing alignment quality.
method: TALCO splits long genome sequences into smaller tiles (chunks processed separately) while keeping memory use constant on the accelerator, regardless of sequence length. The key insight is that different backtracking paths (the steps that retrace an alignment calculation) from different tiles always converge at the same boundary point, which guarantees optimal results even under banding constraints (a technique that limits the search area to speed up computation). This approach works with both classical alignment algorithms like X-Drop and adaptive algorithms like WFA-Adapt.
key_novelty: TALCO uses the fact that backtracking paths converge at tile boundaries to achieve optimal alignments while maintaining constant memory—the first tiling technique that works with adaptive algorithms like WFA-Adapt.
contributions: Novel traceback convergence-based tiling strategy that ensures optimal alignments under banding constraints
First application of tiling to adaptive algorithms (WFA-Adapt), generalizing beyond classical sequence alignment
Software optimization achieving 39-57x memory reduction for X-Drop and WFA-Adapt
ASIC accelerator achieving 1,900-2,000x throughput/watt over CPU while maintaining higher alignment quality than existing baselines

metrics.speedup: 1,900-2,000x throughput/watt over CPU (ASIC); 50x over GPU baselines
metrics.accuracy: Maintains optimal alignment quality under banding; higher quality than existing tiling heuristics

primary_theme: Memory-efficient tiling for optimal genome sequence alignment
